extracted.intended_audience: general readers and those interested in jokes/humor/folklore
extracted.subtask_description: Describing and analyzing the lightbulb joke cycle: its standard Q/A form, typical punch-line content (often stereotyping), variations (puns, topical responses), and social functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the lightbulb joke
rubrics_metrics.description: A lightbulb joke is a joke cycle that asks how many people of a certain group are needed to change, replace, or screw in a light bulb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulates a question naming a target group and expects a punch line about how many members of that group are required; the page gives the canonical template: Q. How many [members of the target group] does it take to change a lightbulb? A. Three — one to hold the light bulb and two to turn the ladder around.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question-and-answer structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke generally takes the form of a Q/A: a 'how many' question followed by a concise punch line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example structure shown on the page; punch line usually numeric and immediately delivers the stereotype-based gag. This concise Q/A form is central to the cycle and its recognizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch line highlights a stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, the punch line answer highlights a stereotype of the target group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous versions satirize cultures, beliefs, occupations, etc.; the stereotype is typically the joke's point (e.g., efficiency, stupidity, drunkenness). The page emphasizes this as the usual mechanism of humor in the cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derogatory tone and targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Lightbulb jokes tend to be derogatory in tone and have been used to insult intelligence or demean groups (e.g., ethnic jokes, jokes about gays and women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical usage in the late 1960s and 1970s often insulted intelligence (Polish jokes cited). The page notes this as a common tone and gives example anti-pattern punch lines that rely on depicting stupidity or incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecating / prideful inversions
rubrics_metrics.description: Targets of the joke may take pride in the stereotypes or originate versions themselves, producing self-deprecating or prideful variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'How many Germans does it take to change a lightbulb? One, we're very efficient but not funny.' The page notes such variants can function to ease tensions between subgroups and sometimes invert the expected insult into internalized pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pun-based variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some versions of the joke are puns on the words 'change' or 'screw'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: 'How many psychiatrists does it take to change a light bulb? None—the light bulb will change when it's ready.' and 'How many flies does it take to screw in a lightbulb? Two, but don't ask me how they got in there.' The page highlights wordplay as an important variation mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical / event-based variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Lightbulb jokes are often responses to contemporary events and can be adapted to current news or crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes jokes referencing power outages and cites a Village Voice contest around the Iran hostage crisis (example punch line: 'You send us the prize money and we'll tell you the answer'). This shows the cycle's adaptability to topical humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/commentary function
rubrics_metrics.description: The cycle can serve satirical or social-commentary roles, reflecting or negotiating intergroup relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly references cited on how lightbulb jokes illuminate social action processes and can be used to ease tensions or make statements about groups and professions; the page situates the joke within folklore and humor studies.
